en: The *Sambandhaparīkṣā* composed by Ācārya Dharmakīrti (accompanied by the commentary composed by Prabhācandra):

Now, since atoms are like iron rods— lacking any mutual connection— and because the cognition of gross objects and the like is therefore erroneous, how could an entity possess that nature [of being gross] on their account?
For instance: would the relation between objects be characterized by dependence, or would it be characterized by the fusion of their forms?
In the first case, would this relation exist between two related entities that have already been established?
Or [is it] between two things that are unestablished?
It cannot be between two unestablished things,
because their own nature does not exist, like the horns of a hare.
Furthermore, since there is an absence of dependence (*pāratantrya*) between two things that have already been established, there is no connection at all.
And it has been said:
"Dependence is indeed a connection; when [the things] are already established, what dependence could there be?"
Therefore, in reality, there is no relation for any entity whatsoever. // 1 //
Nor is this [relation] characterized by the fusion of forms;
for if the two related entities are distinct, there is a contradiction with the fusion of forms,
and if they are one, there is all the more an absence of relation.
Because a relation is impossible in the absence of two related entities, since it must reside in both; or, is their contiguity (*nairantarya*) the physical contact (*rūpaśleṣa*) between them?
No; because this [intermediate state] is unreal by virtue of being an intermediate mode of existence, it is impossible for it to have the nature of a relation.
Furthermore, if uninterruptedness were the nature of a relation, why would even interruptedness not be a relation? Moreover, this contact of forms must be in its entirety.
Or could it be by way of a single part?

If there were a fusion of atoms through their entire essence (*sarvātmanā*), the aggregate would be no larger than a single atom. If there were a fusion of them by way of a single part, are those parts constitutive of its very nature?
Or are they other than it?
If they were identical with it, there could be no spatial contact with matter (*rūpa*), because such identity is absent.
If they are distinct entities,
then regarding the contact of forms between those [atoms] and the atoms— whether by their entire self or by one part— the same objection applies,
and there would be an infinite regress. As it has been said:
For connection consists in the contact of forms; how could that exist when there is duality?
Therefore, in reality, there is no connection between things that are distinct by nature. // 2 //
Furthermore, relation belongs exclusively to other things,
because it resides in two [relata].
And does an entity depend upon that relation while being itself existent or non-existent?
It is not non-existent, because that would contradict its being the locus for the property of dependence, like the horn of a donkey;
nor is it existent, because it is devoid of all objective reference.
Otherwise, it would contradict existence;
therefore, that which is called "dependence on another" cannot be established as a relationship of such a nature.
And it has been said:
For dependence is a relation; how can that which is non-existent depend? And how can an existent thing, which by its very nature is independent of everything else, depend? (3)
Furthermore, is this relation distinct from the two related entities, or non-distinct?
If it were non-distinct, then it would be nothing other than the two related entities themselves.
Is there no relation at all,
or is it that very [relation], or not those two?
If they are distinct;
How could two unrelated entities become related?
Or, even if the relation were a distinct entity,
what would be the relation between those two related entities and that single relation?
Just as there is no relation whatsoever between two related entities due to the aforementioned defects,
so it is here as well.
Therefore, if another relation were admitted between these two, there would be an infinite regress.

Even in that case, because of the consequence of further relations [between the relation and its relata], the cognition of a relation between two related things is not real; for apart from those two, no other relation is possible. As it has been said:
If it is argued that the relation between two things exists because of their connection with a single [third] thing, then what is the relation between those two?
There would be an infinite regress, and likewise, there could be no cognition of a relation.
Therefore—those two entities and everything else besides them all abide within their own selves;
thus, entities are inherently unmixed, yet conceptual construction (kalpanā) mixes them together. // 5 //
Those two entities which are the relata, and the relation which is distinct from them—
all of these abide in their own selves, that is, in their own essential natures.
Therefore, entities are by themselves unmixed, having distinct natures.
Nevertheless, conceptual construction mingles and joins them together. (5)

Therefore, even though there is no real relation between them, users of language, following that very conceptual construction, employ words expressive of action, factors of action (*kāraka*), and so forth, in order to communicate the distinction among entities—which is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—such as: "Devadatta, drive the cow hither, white, with a staff," and so on.
Indeed, there is no connection of the factors of action with the action [in reality].
Because, due to momentariness, the causal factors (kārakas) do not exist at the time of the action; and it has been said:

"And by those who follow that very [momentary sequence], expressive words denoting actions and causal factors are joined together for the purpose of conveying the perception of distinctions among states (bhāva). (Verse 6)

Furthermore, since those two do not exist simultaneously, how can the relation of cause and effect be established? How can a relation, which by nature resides in two things, exist between that which is not dual? (7)
If it is argued that the relation will then be the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), this too is incorrect;
for since cause and effect do not exist simultaneously, that [relation], which must reside in both, is impossible.
Indeed, the effect does not exist at the time of the cause, nor does the cause exist at the time of the effect.
Because the relationship of cause and effect is untenable between two things that exist at the same time, like the left and right horns of a cow.
Therefore, there do not exist two related entities existing simultaneously such that this relation could be present between them.
And when the entity is non-different, the state of being related is simply untenable. // 7 //
An entity existing successively in one place, being independent of others,
does not possess a relation that resides in only one [of the two relata], because even when that [first] entity is absent, the other remains present.
It is also untenable to claim that this relation exists in the effect or the cause sequentially;

for even if the entity called "relation" were to exist sequentially in one [of the two], whether in the cause or the effect, being indifferent to the other—meaning independent of either the cause or the effect—it would not be logical for the relation to reside in only one.
This is because even in the absence of that [relation], the effect and the cause would still exist. // 8 //
If one of those two were to proceed toward the other by depending upon it, then that which is dependent must be a benefactor; but how can that which is non-existent be a benefactor? (9)

If, however, this relation is held to reside in both [terms] by virtue of being "desirous" (saspṛhatva)— in the sense that, depending on one effect or cause, it exists sequentially in another effect or cause—
then it must be assisted by that which is depended upon, because only the beneficiary (upakārya) can depend [on something], and no other.
And how could that which is non-existent provide assistance?

For when the entity called the effect is non-existent at the time of the cause, or when the entity called the cause is non-existent at that [time of the effect], it could not assist at all, because of its lack of capacity. // 9 //
If the causal relationship between those two were due to their connection with a single object,
then it would follow that there is such a relationship between the left and right horns [of a cow] due to their connection with duality and so forth.

Furthermore: if the causal relation between those two things intended as cause and effect arises from their connection with a single object, then that relation would also apply to the left and right horns of a cow, due to their connection with the number two, priority, posteriority, disjunction, and so forth. (10)
For a relation must reside in two things; there is no definition of it other than this.
If causal efficacy (*kāryakāraṇatā*) is [defined as] a connection conditioned by existence and non-existence, [then this is our view]. (11)
If it is argued that [the relationship] is not accepted merely because of a connection with any single one [of the two],
but rather only by way of the definition of a relationship— this is not so, for a relationship is some entity that resides in both [terms].
Apart from this connection with two meanings, there is no other definition for it by which a distinction from number and so forth could be established. // 11 //

Is it not simply those two [the object and the cognition] themselves, associated with a yoga-condition (yogopādhi), that constitute causality here? If you say it is because of their difference, then this word [“causality”] depends upon the one who employs it. // 12 //

If causal relation (*kāryakāraṇatā*) is not every kind of relation, but rather that relation (*yoga* = *sambandha*) which has as its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) or qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) existence when something exists and non-existence when it does not;
then let that very causal relation be those two limiting adjuncts themselves— existence and non-existence.
What is the point of postulating a connection with a non-existent [object]?

If it is argued that they are distinct, then since "existence occurs when there is existence" and "non-existence occurs when there is non-existence," how can many denotable objects be expressed by a single word that denotes a single referent as being in a cause-and-effect relationship?
Is it not the case that this word depends upon the person who employs it?
For the speaker utters a word exactly as he employs it;
thus, even in multiple instances, a single auditory perception is not contradicted, and these two alone constitute the relationship of cause and effect. // 12 //
Even without teachers, people perceive the effect by observing that it occurs when one [cause] is seen and does not occur when that [cause] is not seen. (13)

Because, when one perceives a single thing regarded as a cause, and upon seeing an effect— which is otherwise unperceived despite meeting the conditions for perception— and failing to see it when that [cause] is not seen, people follow the effect and understand, even without instructors, that "this arises from that" or "this is born from that. (13)
Since the cognition of an effect is impossible apart from its perception and non-perception,
even the scriptural mention of "effect" and so forth is employed here for the sake of brevity.

Therefore, perception and non-perception belong to the subject [the cognizer] through a metaphorical attribution to the object; for since the cognition of an effect is impossible apart from existence and non-existence, even the designation "effect" and so forth has been introduced here for the sake of brevity in linguistic usage, with the thought: "Lest the world have to employ such an extensive series of words at every step to express existence and non-existence. // 14 //

The transition to that effect which is described as occurring due to the presence or absence of that [cause] is merely a designation for the object of convention, just as the transition to "cow" occurs based on the dewlap and other such features. (15)
If causal relation is nothing other than positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), how can it be established by means of presence and absence?

As for the understanding of something being the effect of another— which is described as being derived from the mark (*liṅga*) consisting in the absence of that [cause]— and expressed as "this is the effect of that" or "this is the cause of that"—
that is merely a designation for the object of a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).
Just as by the statement "This is a cow because it possesses a dewlap and so forth," the object of the conventional usage "cow" is demonstrated. // 15 //
When an entity exists, its existence occurs; indeed, existence itself is the state of being brought about.
The relationship between cause and effect is established through perception and non-perception. (16)

And since it is well-established through perception and non-perception that causality consists in this: "When the effect is about to come into being—that is, when it possesses the property of coming into existence—the very presence of that which is considered the cause constitutes its causality; and the very presence of that which is considered the effect, when [the cause] exists, constitutes its status as an effect.
Therefore, causality is nothing other than existence and non-existence themselves; there is no other. (16)

Conceptual constructions, which have as their object the sphere of cause and effect and whose true meaning consists merely of this much, manifest objects that are false, as if they were composed of real things. (17)
Therefore, existence and non-existence are merely this much; that object for which these two constitute its reality is "one whose reality consists of this much.

Those conceptual constructions whose objects have such a nature—having this much as their seed—are within the domain of cause and effect, and they display objects as if they were joined, as if connected, even though they are actually unconnected.
And because they are produced in this way, their objects are false. // 17 //

If [the cause] is distinct, what is the connection? And if it is not distinct, how can there even be the relationship of cause and effect? Furthermore, while one thing exists, how could those two be both separated and joined?
Furthermore, is this entity consisting of cause and effect distinct or non-distinct?
If it were distinct;
In that case, if they are distinct, what connection can there be, given that each is established in its own intrinsic nature?
Or if they are non-distinct, then even in the case of non-distinction, how could there be the relationship of cause and effect? It could not exist at all.
It might be argued: "There is no relation between things that are either different or non-different.
What then? It is through being related to a single entity called 'relation'.

To this we reply: even in this case, if there were another relation distinct from existence (*sattā*), then those two things intended as cause and effect, which are currently separate, would have to become joined.
And how are those two related as conjoined and inherent?
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera," [the relationship of] owner and owned and so forth are also included. (18)
By this, all [theories] such as conjunction (*saṃyogin*) and inherence (*samavāyin*) have been examined;
moreover, because they do not mutually benefit one another, there can be no such relationship.

All this has been considered by means of the preceding refutation of a general relation; because conjoined things (*saṃyogin*) and so forth do not assist one another, and because there is no producer-produced relationship, there is no such relation.
For even in the production of an effect, it is not the case that something which is inherent (*samavāyin*) is its producer, because if it were, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). (20)
Now, if it is argued that there exists some inherent relation (*samavāyin*) which produces the effect in the form of a composite whole,
and therefore it is not the case that [the cause] is unrelated due to providing no assistance;
that is not so.
For even when the production of an effect is admitted by some to be through an inherent cause (samavāyin),
that [cause] is not [inherently related] at that time, because the effect has not yet been produced at the moment of its generation.
Nor does the status of being an inherent cause become established merely from that act of generating.
Otherwise, it would follow that even a potter and others would be the inherent cause (samavāyin) of the jar. // 20 //

If a relation were to exist even when there is no mutual benefit between those two, or in inherence, or with respect to something else, then the entire universe would be in a state of mutual inherence.

If a relation is asserted between those two inherent entities even though they do not mutually benefit one another—whether because the inherence is eternal, or because the inherence does not benefit them, or because they do not benefit anything else—then the entire universe would be inherently related to one another despite lacking mutual connection. // 21 //

Even if conjunction were produced [in them], those two would not be the possessors of that conjunction; for they would then incur the status of being agents of action and so forth, and their stability has already been refuted. (22)
Thus ends the *Sambandhaparīkṣā* composed by the Master Dharmakīrti.

Furthermore, if it is argued that those two possess the state of being conjoined because conjunction is an effect produced by them, then even in the production of that conjunction, [the two] would be required;
therefore, they do not become conjoined merely through the production of conjunction.
Otherwise, action itself would incur the status of being a conjoined entity;
for conjunction is held to be produced by the action of one or by the action of both.
Furthermore, by the inclusion of the word "etcetera," conjunction itself would also possess the status of being a conjoined entity.

If it is argued that "possession of conjunction" does not arise from the production of a conjunction, but rather from its establishment— that is, from its persistence— we reply: no, for persistence has already been explained [and] rejected in another treatise.
Since there is no relationship of produced and producer between the supported and the supporter, there is no other mode of existence [for them]. // 22 //
Thus ends the commentary on the *Sambandhaparīkṣā* composed by Prabhācandra.
